title: My own fruit
hook: the rational soul sees itself, shapes itself, and gathers its own fruit (Meditations 11.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was schoolmaster: even a good, gentle person leaves someone relieved. Your line was lightly.

An apple tree grows an apple, and someone else eats it. A cow makes milk, and someone else drinks it. A vine grows grapes for somebody's table. Plants and animals, Marcus says, bear fruit that others enjoy. Book eleven of the Meditations opens with him noticing one kind of fruit that's different, one harvest that stays with the one who grows it.
screen: `AN APPLE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `BOOK ELEVEN OPENS.` → `MY OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: First, the mirror. The reasoning soul, Marcus says, sees itself, examines itself, and shapes itself into whatever it chooses. No plant can look at itself and decide to grow differently. We can. Second, the fruit. The fruit it bears, he says, it gathers for itself. A tree's fruit and an animal's yield are enjoyed by others. But the fruit of a well-lived life, steadiness, kindness, clear sight, belongs to the one who grew it. You don't have to wait for someone else to taste it. Third, whole at every point. A dance or a play, Marcus says, is left incomplete if it's cut off partway. But the soul reaches its own end wherever life stops. Each act done well is whole in itself, so at any moment it can say: I have what is my own. Fourth, the wide view. The soul ranges over the whole universe and the emptiness around it, stretches into endless time, and sees that those who come after us will see nothing new. A person of forty, he adds, with any understanding at all, has in a sense seen everything that has been and will be: the same patterns keep coming round. And closer to home, look honestly at yourself, and the harvest is already yours.
screen: `IT SEES AND SHAPES ITSELF.` · `IT GATHERS ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `WHOLE WHEREVER IT STOPS.` · `THE WIDE VIEW OF TIME.` · then, large: `MY OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Look at yourself for a minute the way you'd look at a friend you love, not judging, just seeing, and name one fruit you grew this week: patience in one place, a kept promise, a kind word at the right time. Gather it yourself, without waiting for anyone else to notice. Then notice one thing you'd like to shape differently, and simply set the intention.
Marcus, who said the reasoning soul sees itself, shapes itself, and gathers its own harvest, whole at every point. Today's word.
Your line: gather your own harvest. Nobody else has to taste it for it to be real. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations end the day with a short, honest look at themselves, naming one good thing they grew and one thing to shape differently tomorrow.

Meditations.meaning: the private notebook of reflections Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself

book eleven.meaning: the eleventh of the twelve books of the Meditations

reasoning soul.meaning: Marcus's name for the part of us that thinks and chooses

notes: 11.1 paraphrased: the properties of the rational soul (sees itself, analyzes itself, makes itself as it chooses, enjoys its own fruit); unlike a dance or play, it completes its purpose wherever life ends ('I have what is my own'); it traverses the universe and the void, stretches into infinite time, sees that posterity will see nothing new; the man of forty. Confirm.
Marcus was born AD 121 and most scholars date the Meditations to the 170s, so 'well past forty' is safe; confirm.
